bounded_proposition: Around 1400 Great Zimbabwe was a hierarchical political/economic center supported by household production, tribute/extraction, reciprocal/dependency relations and organized collective labor. Slavery existed in the connected coastal network, but current evidence does not establish slavery/enslavement at Great Zimbabwe or Great-Zimbabwe-specific slave-trade participation.
required_abstention: Do not infer forced/slave labor from monumentality, hierarchy, tribute or dependency; do not back-project later Mutapa/Torwa servants/slaves; do not transfer Kilwa/Sofala slavery to Great Zimbabwe; do not infer absence from collective labor.
evidence_locus: Great Zimbabwe capital/site; surrounding production landscape; Save/Sofala corridor as broad trade context; Kilwa 1331 as separate connected slavery locus
inference_extent: Positive site-level political economy/labor context; slavery at site and target-specific slave-trade participation remain unresolved; no state-wide practice inference.
law_practice_note: No exact-anchor Great Zimbabwe written slave/status law recovered; archaeology and specialist political-economy reconstruction support labor organization/dependency but not a slave-status designation.
network_territorial_note: Great Zimbabwe participates in Indian Ocean commodity networks and connected Kilwa contains slavery near anchor, but connectivity does not establish Great Zimbabwe captive provenance or export.
historical_terms: communal work party; reciprocal labor; tribute; subject homestead; dependency; servants/slaves in later comparator; enslaved people at Kilwa
category_mapping_note: Tribute, political dependency and communal labor are not automatically slavery; later servants/slaves and connected coastal slavery remain temporally/spatially separate.
language_access_limitations: English specialist scholarship and translated Ibn Battuta reviewed; no independent Arabic edition or exhaustive Shona/Portuguese source review; Scite cross-check unavailable due quota.
geometry_unresolved_note: Great Zimbabwe site may be a navigation locus after separate geometry review; no political-hinterland or slavery-practice polygon is authorized.

bounded_proposition: Traditional/pre-contact Māori society included war-captive unfree statuses described through taurekareka/mōkai and commonly mapped to slavery/captivity. This applies to the social world surrounding the 1700 anchor, but exact distribution, prevalence, terminology and status rules across individual iwi/hapū remain unresolved.
required_abstention: Do not treat Māori as one 1700 polity; do not infer uniformity across iwi/hapū; do not map taurekareka/mōkai automatically to Atlantic chattel slavery; do not collapse dependent hapū/tribute into slave status; do not back-project Musket Wars scale/economics; do not infer every battle produced captives.
evidence_locus: Multiple traditional Māori community/source traditions; early-contact observations; later customary-law reconstruction across iwi/hapū contexts
inference_extent: Positive period/institution-level war-captive unfreedom; aggregate exact-1700 distribution and prevalence withheld.
law_practice_note: No single written Aotearoa-wide law; customary status reconstructed from oral tradition, early observers, ethnography and specialist synthesis. Institutional reality does not imply a uniform legal regime.
network_territorial_note: Captive movement can follow intergroup warfare, but no Aotearoa-wide slave-trade network or territorial prevalence is inferred.
historical_terms: taurekareka; mōkai; rangatira; tūtūā; tāngata; war captive; dependent hapū
category_mapping_note: Taurekareka is commonly rendered slave but the Waitangi Tribunal cautions that the translation is not entirely accurate; mōkai is broader/contextual; dependent tāngata/tribute relations remain separate.
language_access_limitations: English-language specialist/institutional syntheses and translated/edited early-contact sources reviewed; no exhaustive Māori-language oral-history corpus or iwi-by-iwi reconstruction; Scite cross-check unavailable due quota.
geometry_unresolved_note: Aotearoa or modern iwi boundaries cannot become a uniform 1700 practice polygon; any future geometry must be claim/member-locus specific.

bounded_proposition: Around 500 CE the early Nobatian/Ballana royal sphere in Lower Nubia practiced human retainer sacrifice, demonstrating lethal coercion attached to royal mortuary practice. The sacrificed people's slave status, wider Nobatian slaveholding prevalence and external slave-trade participation remain unresolved.
required_abstention: Do not equate sacrificed retainer with slave; do not transfer Blemmyes practice from Procopius; do not back-project the 652 baqṭ or later Christian Nubia; do not infer polity-wide prevalence or an external trade from royal cemeteries.
evidence_locus: Qustul and Ballana royal cemeteries in Lower Nubia; broader Middle Nile slavery historiography; Philae textual boundary context
inference_extent: Positive royal-site coerced-death practice near anchor; slave status and polity-wide/external-trade extent withheld.
law_practice_note: No exact-anchor Nobatian legal/status corpus recovered; archaeology directly supports sacrificial practice but not juridical slave status.
network_territorial_note: Broader Middle Nile slavery/slave-taking is contextual; significant early external slave trade is not securely demonstrated and no Nobatia-500 trade network is assigned.
historical_terms: human sacrifice; retainer sacrifice; attendant/servant; slave; captive; slave-taking; external slave trade
category_mapping_note: Human retainer sacrifice is a secure practice category; older labels of sacrificed attendants as slaves are not adopted without independent status evidence.
language_access_limitations: English specialist archaeology/history and translated Procopius reviewed; no exhaustive Greek/Coptic/Old Nubian corpus; Scite cross-check unavailable due quota.
geometry_unresolved_note: Qustul/Ballana may serve as evidence loci after separate geometry review; no Nobatia-wide practice polygon is authorized.
